processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas: withered, shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: dark, twisted strips.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges.
taste_profile: Named for its aroma: a seller describes a milky note mixed with flowers and fruit. Beyond that, expect the roast and mineral weight of the class.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas. Smell the lid after each pour, since that is where the milky note is said to show.

vintage_note: Sold in small lots by spring harvest year and roast, as is usual for Wuyi famous bushes. Ask for the year, the roast and the growing area.
description:
Shi Ru Xiang, also sold as Shi Ru, is a Wuyi bush named for its fragrance, in the same way that Rou Gui and Bai She Xiang are.

Its making follows the class: shaking, partial oxidation and a roast. A heavy roast could easily cover a delicate note, so ask about the fire.

A seller writes of milky aromas with flowers and fruit. These are tasting notes, not measurements, and lots differ. Brew it hot and short.

The name Shi Ru also appears on lists of Song and Yuan tribute tea. Do not assume a lot on sale descends from it unless the seller can show more.
history:
Chinese accounts of Wuyi tea group Shi Ru Xiang with bushes named for their aroma type, and a modern roll of Wuyi famous bushes lists it. Where and when this bush was first recorded is not well documented.

A tea called Shi Ru appears on lists of Song and Yuan tribute tea, and one account says Kublai Khan admired it. Whether today's bush descends from that tea is unproven.
